analysis.one_liner: Bans grease-proof PFAS chemicals in food packaging starting January 2024.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in committee when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal food-safety law to make it illegal to sell or ship food packaging containing intentionally added PFAS (man-made "forever chemicals" often used to keep grease from soaking through wrappers and takeout boxes). PFAS do not break down in the body or the environment, and the ban would take effect on January 1, 2024. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, where it stayed until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers who eat packaged, takeout, and fast food, since nearly everyone is exposed to PFAS through food contact materials, would face less direct exposure. Makers of PFAS-free food packaging would gain a guaranteed market once treated packaging is banned.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Food consumers and PFAS-free packaging makers

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a federal violation to introduce food packaging with intentionally added PFAS into interstate commerce, using FDA's food-safety enforcement authority.
Gives packaging makers and food sellers more than two years to reformulate, since the ban applies beginning January 1, 2024.

analysis.who_pays: Chemical companies that produce PFAS and food-packaging manufacturers that rely on PFAS coatings for grease resistance would bear reformulation and compliance costs; some costs could be passed through to restaurants and food prices.

drawbacks.text: Packaging manufacturers and their chemical suppliers would face real reformulation and compliance costs, and some of that cost could be passed on to food sellers and consumers.

The bill defines PFAS broadly (any man-made substance with at least one fully fluorinated carbon atom), which is a strict, chemistry-based definition that could capture more compounds than the narrow grease-proofing uses most commonly discussed.
It does not fund alternatives testing or safety review of substitute coatings, so compliance burden falls on industry without public support for the transition.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health benefit of reducing a persistent, accumulating chemical in contact with food is broad and durable, while the cost is a one-time reformulation that packaging makers have already demonstrated is feasible in many product lines. The bill is narrow (it targets packaging only, not all PFAS uses) and includes a generous phase-in, making the tradeoff favorable, though the broad PFAS definition could have created edge-case compliance disputes.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee the day after introduction, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 18, 2021 by Rep. Debbie Dingell with Rep. Don Young as an original bipartisan cosponsor.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and the next day to the Subcommittee on Health.
It drew 22 cosponsors, 19 Democrats and 3 Republicans, but no further action was taken on it.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill died without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PFAS producers and food-packaging makers avoided a January 2024 federal ban on PFAS-treated packaging, and consumers gained nothing because the exposure the bill targeted was never eliminated.

for.name: Rep. Debbie Dingell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban intentionally added PFAS in food packaging.

for.name: Rep. Don Young
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as its lead Republican cosponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action, never scheduling a markup or moving it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan at introduction, with a Democratic sponsor and a Republican original cosponsor, and its 22 cosponsors split 19-3 Democratic; there were no votes, so no party-line pattern on the merits was ever recorded.

industries.note: A federal ban on intentionally added PFAS in food packaging eliminates a market for PFAS production used in food-contact materials. Their interest in the bill's failure ran against reducing consumer exposure.

industries.industry: Food packaging and paper manufacturers using PFAS grease-proofing
industries.note: These suppliers would have had to reformulate or drop treated products by January 2024. Continuing to sell treated packaging keeps a persistent chemical in contact with consumers' food.
A 2024 ban would have locked in demand for substitute coatings and untreated packaging, putting alternative suppliers on the winning side of consumer health interests.
Chains would bear switching and cost pass-through, but removing PFAS from their packaging aligns with what their customers want.
